title: Phoebe and the Pumpkin Plunge
markdown:
Dawn burst gold and pink through Phoebe Ash’s window. Sunlight arrived thick as melted butter. Birds trilled like a thousand tiny trumpets. Phoebe stretched, tweed already perfect, eyes already sharp. A tingle tickled her toes. Today felt electric, the sort of morning that hid a claim in its pocket. Then a letter buzzed in: mechanical whir, a puff of steam, a polite click on the sill.

Urgent summons from Mr. Lark, her most enthusiastic client. Big dreams. Bigger inventions. Insured chaos as a lifestyle. His new Automated Biscuit Butterer had a “minor problem.” Phoebe knew minor, with Lark, meant butter in the rafters and a very specific clause about condiments.

She skipped the cobbles, umbrella tapping a jaunty beat. Imagine! A machine that buttered biscuits! Fantastic. The street smelled of coal and bakery. She rounded the corner. Pop! Sticky marmalade fragments rained from an upstairs window, orange jewels with a talent for hair. His workshop, of course. She flicked her wrist, dodged the shower, and burst through the door expecting a sugary battlefield: crumbs in drifts, butter on the ceiling, perhaps a biscuit still in flight.

But the battlefield had been tidied into a philosophy. Mr. Lark stood calm, goggles smudged, hair miraculously contained, holding one perfectly buttered biscuit aloft as if it were a medal. “Ah, Phoebe! A perfect specimen. A tiny hiccup in the part that controlled how thick the butter was. A mere trifle!” In the corner, tragically singed prototypes lay like edible casualties of an over-enthusiastic oven. “Insured, of course.” He patted a ticking ledger that seemed to vibrate with self-importance. “Top-tier coverage for butter-related mishaps. Even spontaneous baking disasters, within reason.”

Therefore she noted the policy, sketched the thickness-control part, pocketed a crumb of evidence, and did not linger. Lark was already humming. Humming, in her experience, preceded the next machine.

Later that week the Grand Exhibition hall buzzed with polish and possibility, clinking teacups, hushed bets, the particular hush of people who wanted to see something go wrong and call it progress. Center stage: Mr. Lark again, and the Personal Puddle Jumper, a contraption of copper pipes, coiled spring-boots, and parasol frames welded into optimism. “No more damp socks!” he boomed. “Press this button. Leap elegantly over any puddle, however deep or deceptively innocent!”

A frankly pathetic puddle had been provided on a tarpaulin, as if water needed encouragement.

Phoebe watched from the front row. A familiar knot tickled her throat. Lark’s demonstrations were legendary, and not always for the reasons he intended. He beamed, tapped the polished button.

Thwump!

The springs coiled with alarming speed. But the Jumper, designed for pedestrian puddles, had grander ambitions. Mr. Lark launched himself not over a frankly pathetic puddle, but straight up. He spun, a blur of tweed and flyaway hair, past chandeliers, past a prize-winning stoic parrot, and with a magnificent bubbly sploosh landed in the award-winning giant pumpkin.

Foam rose in a pleasant cascade that smelled faintly of prize marrow. The hall gasped. Then it roared. Magnificent! Seeds decorated hats. The parrot, still stoic, acquired a bubble.

Therefore Phoebe unrolled her clipboard, pen poised, professional in a room of seeds. She had already begun the sentence about unconventional landings. Mr. Lark emerged spluttering, grinning, foamy, affectionate toward the dented gourd. “A slight over-enthusiasm in the propulsion system, perhaps?” He patted the pumpkin. It made a wet, forgiving sound.

“Mr. Lark,” she said, steady, “about this Puddle Jumper’s policy. The landing is rather unconventional.”

But he was already pulling a crumpled napkin from his pocket, mind miles ahead of the foam. “Don’t you worry! Next invention: automatic tea-making and self-folding laundry. The Domestic Dynamo! Perfectly brewed tea. Socks that fold themselves!”

Therefore Phoebe Ash adjusted her spectacles, a new claim already sparkling, and grinned hard enough to power a small city. Today was going to be spectacular. She tapped her umbrella once, turned toward the door, and went looking for the next insured disaster before the tea had even been invented.
characters: Phoebe Ash (insurance investigator), Mr. Lark (serial inventor)
author: StoryGen Community
